title: Amazon to Add 300,000 Holiday Workers, Bucking Retail Hiring Slump - BigGo Finance
text:
Amazon to Add 300,000 Holiday Workers, Bucking Retail Hiring Slump — BigGo Finance Ask AI Real-time News Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast Earnings Call Event Calendar Watchlist Podcast More Ask AI Real-time News Watchlist Holdings Market Earnings Call Event Calendar Podcast Amazon to Add 300,000 Holiday Workers, Bucking Retail Hiring Slump
 Add preferred source Amazon will hire more than 300,000 seasonal, part-time and full-time workers across its U.S. operations network for the holiday season, a 20% increase from last year and its first expansion of holiday recruitment in three years. The company will pay seasonal staff about $20 an hour on average and, starting Jan. 1, 2027, extend full-time-level health coverage to seasonal employees working at least 30 hours a week. The move contrasts with a broader retail pullback: Challenger, Gray & Christmas expects total U.S. holiday hiring below 450,000, the lowest since 2008, and Walmart and Target have not published companywide targets. The National Retail Federation forecasts holiday sales up 4.2% to $1.013 trillion. Key Elements 
 Amazon.com Inc National Retail Federation Challenger, Gray & Christmas Walmart Target UPS Andy Jassy Andy Challenger Whole Foods Market First Tech Federal Credit Union Amazon.com Inc (AMZN) plans to bring on more than 300,000 seasonal, part-time and full-time workers across its U.S. operations network for the year-end shopping rush, a roughly 20% increase over last year and the first time in three years the company has enlarged its holiday hiring pool.
 The Seattle-based e-commerce and cloud giant said Tuesday that postings will roll out weekly from October through December at fulfillment centers, sortation hubs and delivery stations nationwide. For the prior three holiday seasons, Amazon held seasonal recruitment at 250,000. The new total adds about 50,000 positions.
 The move runs against the direction of the broader retail labor market. Outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas expects total U.S. holiday hiring to come in below 450,000 this year, which would be the weakest seasonal recruitment since 2008. Walmart (WMT) and Target (TGT) have again declined to publish companywide holiday hiring targets, a sharp break from the aggressive staffing pushes of the pandemic years.
 "For the past three years, almost every hiring announcement we've seen has been smaller and more surgical than the pre-pandemic playbook," said Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at the Chicago-based firm.
 Amazon is pairing the expansion with higher pay and richer benefits. Seasonal operations staff will earn an average of about $20 an hour, while full-time core operations employees start at a minimum of $20 an hour and average close to $24. Counting benefits, Amazon puts average total compensation for full-time operations staff above $32 an hour. The company has committed more than $1.5 billion to wage increases for its U.S. operations workforce.
 Starting Jan. 1, 2027, seasonal employees who average at least 30 hours a week will be eligible for the same medical coverage offered to regular full-time staff, with plans starting at $5 a week and a $5 copay for office visits. Workers hired before that date gain coverage on Jan. 1; those starting on or after it are covered from day one. Previously, seasonal and some part-time staff typically faced a 90-day waiting period, which for short holiday assignments often meant no coverage at all before the job ended.
 Other perks include uncapped 10% discounts on eligible groceries and household goods bought online at Amazon.com and Whole Foods Market, and 20% off in-store at Whole Foods, stackable with existing Prime member offers. Amazon is also preparing a financial services program, Day 1 Financial, with First Tech Federal Credit Union, offering low-cost banking products to eligible employees and their families, with a phased launch beginning late this year and wider availability in 2027. Members would keep access even after leaving the company.
 Demand signals support the staffing bet. The National Retail Federation forecast last week that U.S. retail sales in November and December will rise 4.2% from a year earlier to $1.013 trillion, the first time the holiday season has topped $1 trillion and an acceleration from last year's 3.1% gain to $972 billion. Adobe projects online spending of $275.1 billion in the two months, up 6.7% from 2025. EMarketer estimates that nearly 40 cents of every online dollar spent in the U.S. goes to Amazon.
 Amazon's own results point the same way. Paid unit sales worldwide rose 17% in the second quarter, up from 12% a year earlier, and Chief Executive Andy Jassy has said Prime members received record delivery speeds in the first half, with same-day or overnight shipments up more than 40% year over year.
 The hiring increase also reflects physical growth. Amazon said the expansion of its U.S. network, including newly opened sites, is part of the reason for the larger intake, not just holiday order volume.
 The contrast with rivals is stark. UPS (UPS) plans to take on more than 100,000 seasonal workers, about 9% fewer than a year ago, as it trims Amazon volume to focus on higher-margin business. Amazon has steadily shifted more parcels onto its own delivery network, reducing what it hands to outside carriers.
 Metric Figure 
 Amazon holiday hires (2026) More than 300,000 
 Amazon holiday hires (prior three years) 250,000 
 Seasonal average hourly wage About $20 
 Full-time core operations average hourly wage Nearly $24 
 Full-time total compensation including benefits Above $32 per hour 
 Wage investment commitment Over $1.5 billion 
 NRF holiday sales forecast (Nov-Dec) $1.013 trillion, up 4.2% 
 Challenger holiday hiring forecast Below 450,000, lowest since 2008 
 UPS seasonal hiring plan More than 100,000, down about 9% 
 Note: Wage and compensation figures are Amazon's own disclosures. Sales forecast is from the National Retail Federation.
 The expansion sits alongside continued corporate cost-cutting. Amazon trimmed several hundred retail roles this month, affecting customer service, seller support and retail engineering teams, after cutting about 16,000 corporate positions in January. The company has shed roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since October 2025, even as total headcount reached about 1.6 million as of June 30, up 3% from a year earlier excluding contractors and temporary staff.
 For investors, the larger seasonal intake cuts both ways. It signals confidence in fourth-quarter order volume, but it also raises short-term labor costs, and the health-coverage change adds to benefit expenses from 2027. Amazon reports third-quarter results on Oct. 29. Wall Street expects adjusted earnings of $1.96 a share on revenue of $202.2 billion, according to TipRanks, with a consensus rating of Strong Buy across 44 analysts and an average price target of $330.49. The stock rose 0.54% on Tuesday.
 Walmart's decision last week to broaden health benefits for its own workforce underscores how medical costs have become a pressure point for U.S. households contending with persistent inflation, and Amazon's seasonal coverage change lands in that same debate.
